title: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” — who is the king of Psalm 45, and who is called “God”?
summary: Psalm 45 is spoken “touching the king”. At verse 6 a king is addressed as “O God”, and at verse 7 “God, thy God” has anointed him. The verses quoted do not name the king, and Hebrews 1:8 applies the same words to “the Son”.
text: KJV Psalms 45:1: “My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.” KJV 45:2: “Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever.” KJV 45:6: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.” KJV 45:7: “Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” KJV Hebrews 1:8: “But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” Hebrew (WLC) 45:7: כִּסְאֲךָ֣ אֱ֭לֹהִים עֹולָ֣ם וָעֶ֑ד. Brenton’s Greek 44:7: Ὁ θρόνος σου ὁ Θεὸς εἰς αἰῶνα αἰῶνος. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/45/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA044.htm.
reasoning: The psalm is a song “touching the king” and goes on to speak to him. What the verses do not say is who the king is, or in what sense the one addressed is “God” and yet is anointed by “God, thy God”. The answer decides whether the verse addresses a human king of the psalm’s time, God, or one who is both addressed and anointed.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that the king is a human king of the psalmist’s time and is addressed as “God” in an honorific sense; that the words of verse 6 turn from the king to God; that the king is a figure for one still to come; and that the verse is read as Hebrews 1:8 reads it, of “the Son”. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them. The Hebrew quoted has no verb between “thy throne” and “God”, so the clause can be taken in more than one way, and this record does not say which. Hebrews 1:8 introduces the words with “unto the Son he saith”, so it gives its own application; it does not say who the king was for the psalm’s first singers. The psalm’s title is not in the packaged KJV and was not examined for this record. A separate record compares the Greek of 45:13. The psalm is verse. Check made: Psalms 45:1, 45:2, 45:6 and 45:7 and Hebrews 1:8 were read in the packaged KJV; no other book was searched. Brenton’s Greek numbers this psalm 44 (KJV Psalm 45); the Hebrew and the Greek run one verse ahead of the KJV. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: “It was thou, a man mine equal” — who is the friend who turned against the speaker in Psalm 55?
summary: The speaker of Psalm 55 says the one who did him harm was not an enemy but “a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance”, with whom he “took sweet counsel together”. The verses quoted do not name the man or say what he did.
text: KJV Psalms 55:12: “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him:” KJV 55:13: “But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.” KJV 55:14: “We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company.” KJV 55:20: “He hath put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him: he hath broken his covenant.” KJV 55:21: “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.” Hebrew (WLC) 55:14: וְאַתָּ֣ה אֱנֹ֣ושׁ כְּעֶרְכִּ֑י אַ֝לּוּפִ֗י וּמְיֻדָּֽעִי. Brenton’s Greek 54:14: Σὺ δὲ ἄνθρωπε ἰσόψυχε, ἡγεμών μου καὶ γνωστέ μου. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/55/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA054.htm.
reasoning: The man is described by three relations (equal, guide, acquaintance) and two shared acts (counsel, going to the house of God), and is then charged with having “put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him” and broken “his covenant”. The verses give no name, no office and no event, so it is not stated who the man is or what the breach was.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that the man is one named person known to the speaker, whom the verses leave unnamed; that “thou” is a figure for a class of friends who betray; and that verses 20–21 speak of a different person from verses 12–14. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, and this record asserts none. The speaker is not named in the verses quoted, and the psalm’s title is not in the packaged KJV and was not examined for this record. The psalm is verse. title: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living” — what book is this, and what is lost when a name is blotted out?
summary: Psalm 69:28 asks that “them” be blotted out of “the book of the living” and “not be written with the righteous”. The verses quoted do not say what the book is or what follows from a name being removed.
text: KJV Psalms 69:27: “Add iniquity unto their iniquity: and let them not come into thy righteousness.” KJV 69:28: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.” Hebrew (WLC) 69:29: יִ֭מָּחֽוּ מִסֵּ֣פֶר חַיִּ֑ים וְעִ֥ם צַ֝דִּיקִ֗ים אַל־יִכָּתֵֽבוּ. Brenton’s Greek 68:29: Ἐξαλειφθήτωσαν ἐκ βίβλου ζώντων, καὶ μετὰ δικαίων μὴ γραφήτωσαν. KJV Exodus 32:32: “blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written” KJV Exodus 32:33: “Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book” KJV Philippians 4:3: “whose names are in the book of life” KJV Revelation 20:12: “another book was opened, which is the book of life” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/69/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA068.htm.
reasoning: The request pairs two clauses: blotted out of “the book of the living”, and “not … written with the righteous”. What is lost depends on what the book is: a record of who is alive, a list of the righteous, or a record of those whom God counts for life. The verses of the psalm name neither the keeper nor the book’s other contents, and do not say whether blotting out concerns this life or another.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that the book is a register of the living, so that being blotted out is death; that it is a list of those counted among the righteous, as the second clause may suggest; and that it is the book of Exodus 32:32–33, from which a name is blotted for sin. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, and this record asserts none. Exodus 32:32–33, Philippians 4:3 and Revelation 20:12 are quoted as context: they name a book that God has written, a book of life, and the book of life, and they do not say that any of these is the book of Psalm 69:28. Check made: Psalm 69:27–28 was read, and the packaged KJV was searched for the phrases “book of the living” (this verse only) and “book of life” (eight verses, in Philippians and Revelation).
